microphones/polar-patterns/❤️-cardioid.h.title: ❤️ Cardioid
microphones/polar-patterns/❤️-cardioid.h.icon: <svg class="svg-icon lucide-file" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6 22a2 2 0 0 1-2-2V4a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h8a2.4 2.4 0 0 1 1.704.706l3.588 3.588A2.4 2.4 0 0 1 20 8v12a2 2 0 0 1-2 2z"></path><path d="M14 2v5a1 1 0 0 0 1 1h5"></path></svg>
microphones/polar-patterns/❤️-cardioid.h.description:
0º90º180º270º
The cardioid pattern gets its name from its heart-shaped pickup pattern.
It captures sound predominantly from the front, while rejecting most sound from the rear.
Offers moderate rejection of sound from the sides.
It exhibits the proximity effect, meaning that the bass response increases as the sound source gets closer to the microphone.
✔ Live sound reinforcement – Common in vocal mics to reduce feedback from stage monitors.
✔ Recording studios – Ideal for isolating vocals or instruments by reducing background noise.
✔ Broadcasting & podcasting – Helps eliminate room noise and reflections.
✔ Close-miking – Used for individual instruments in loud environments (e.g., drum kits, guitar amps).
The Shure SM58, one of the most famous microphones in the world, has a cardioid pattern.
The proximity effect can be used creatively by singers and voiceover artists to enhance the low-end warmth of their voice.
Supercardioid and hypercardioid patterns are tighter variations of cardioid, offering more directionality but picking up some sound from the rear.

microphones/polar-patterns/⭕️-omnidirect.title: ⭕️ Omnidirectional

microphones/polar-patterns/⭕️-omnidirect.description:
0º90º180º270º
Captures sound equally from all directions (360° around the microphone).
No proximity effect, making it ideal for natural-sounding recordings.
More resistant to wind noise and plosives compared to directional mics.
Typically provides a flatter frequency response than directional microphones.
✔ Studio recording – Used for capturing natural room ambiance.
✔ Lavalier microphones – Frequently used in TV, theater, and interviews.
✔ Classical music recording – Often used in orchestral and choir recordings to preserve natural room acoustics.
✔ Boundary microphones – Used on conference tables or in stage performances.
The first microphones were naturally omnidirectional until engineers developed directional designs.
Omnidirectional microphones work well underwater and are used in hydrophones for underwater recordings.
Many lavalier (clip-on) microphones are omnidirectional to capture speech without worrying about mic positioning.

microphones/polar-patterns/8️⃣-figure-of.description:
0º90º180º270º
Picks up sound equally from the front and rear, while rejecting sound from the sides.
Exhibits the strongest proximity effect of all polar patterns.
Common in ribbon microphones and some large-diaphragm condensers.
More susceptible to off-axis coloration, meaning sound sources must be well-positioned.
✔ Studio recording – Used for stereo recording techniques (Mid-Side and Blumlein pair).
✔ Podcasting & interviews – Allows two people to speak into the same mic from opposite sides.
✔ Live sound for acoustic instruments – Captures both the instrument and room reflections for a natural feel.
✔ Broadcasting – Used in some radio stations where announcers face each other.
The first-ever microphones (carbon microphones) had a figure-of-eight pattern.
Ribbon microphones, like the Royer R-121, naturally have a figure-of-eight pattern due to their ribbon diaphragm design.
The Blumlein stereo technique, invented by Alan Blumlein, uses two figure-of-eight microphones at 90° to each other to create a realistic stereo image.

microphones/stereo-techniques/ebs.html.description: (Equal Brilliance Stereo) Description: Two cardioid microphones positioned at a 90° angle, spaced 25 cm apart. This technique is designed to maintain equal brilliance across the stereo field, providing a balanced frequency response while preserving stereo width and localisation.Tips for Competency: ✔ Ensure precise spacing—25 cm between microphone capsules to achieve optimal stereo imaging. ✔ Use high-quality cardioid microphones to capture a detailed, focused stereo field. ✔ Best for small ensembles, solo instruments, and speech recordings where natural tonal balance is important. ✔ Test different angles and placements based on room acoustics to prevent excessive phase issues. ✔ Avoid excessive off-axis colouration—positioning the microphones at the correct 90° angle ensures an even frequency response across the stereo image.https://sengpielaudio.com/EBS-StereoSystemEnglish.htm

✔ Use a mic bar with pre-measured spacing for accuracy.
✔ Works well for orchestras, choirs, and ambient recordings.

microphones/stereo-techniques/oss.html.description:
OSS (Optimised Stereo Signal) / Jecklin DiskDescription: Two omnidirectional microphones placed 17 cm apart, with an acoustic baffle (disk) between them to enhance spatial separation and reduce phase issues.Tips for Competency:
✔ Ensure precise spacing—17 cm between mics and a properly designed disk (approx. 35 cm in diameter with sound-absorbing material).
✔ Positioning matters—keep the disk perpendicular to the sound source for an accurate stereo image.
✔ Best for natural stereo depth in acoustic and classical recordings.
✔ Avoid using in close-mic setups—this technique works best in well-balanced environments with natural reverb.
✔ Use quality omnidirectional mics to capture a smooth frequency response.

microphones/stereo-techniques/spaced-pai.description:
(A/B)Description: Two omnidirectional microphones spaced apart, often 40 cm to 1 m or more.Tips for Competency:
✔ Best for capturing a wide, immersive stereo image.
✔ Be aware of phase issues—check the 3:1 rule (space mics three times the distance from the source).
✔ Works well for room ambiance, large ensembles, and drum overheads.

protools/topics-pt/playlist-take-compila.description:
Have a track in ProTools that has three or more recordings as playlists(multiple takes)
Create and select a new empty playlist as a master edit destination, which will form the final edit
Change the track to the 'Playlist' view, and observe your previously recorded playlists as folded out tracks
in the image above, the last playlist is being auditioned, the green button indicates this, officially titled 'Solo Comp Lane' Use the green listen button, play through, promoting the preferred selections to the main edit playlist Repeat with each recording. You can rotate a selection through the playlists with Shift + Alt + Command + Up/Down Arrow. Start with the most recent take, which may well have been the best? Work through each track linearly. Delete anything unusable Copy anything definite to the target playlist Continue appraising the other takes, removing unwanted and filling the gaps in the main edit until satisfied.
